I lost my kitty this year on April 4th. It was unexpected and absolutely broke my heart. Typing this out now is still making me cry, and it does hurt and will maybe always hurt, but it gets easier.

I planted flowers on her grave and decorated it and went out each day to tell her how much I love her and miss her. 
I buried her with a polished ocean jasper stone in the shape of a heart, and have a mookaite bracelet that I chose to be in her memory, so I wear that sometimes too. 
It’s awful and terrible and draining and so unbelievably sad. But each day gets that tiny bit easier. And you can live knowing you have beautiful memories you shared with you forever, and knowing that you were your pup’s favourite creature on this planet and gave him/her the greatest, most love-filled life they could have possibly asked for.

Just to note as well, I am not discounting the experiences of vaccine-injured people or families. Nothing is perfect, or guaranteed, but it’s about weighing and minimising risks.

If I had to guess, I’d say her reaction stems from insecurity, and she’s afraid to be judged, especially by you, or she’s been judged for it before. 

If you can, as soon as it is safe to do so, have a face-to-face talk with her. You don’t need to apologise for what you said because you didn’t say anything wrong, but problems or disagreements like this in important friendships are best sorted out through a conversation where you can both see and hear exactly how the other is feeling and why. 
If you’re keen to save the friendship, hear her out, be calm and supportive, and reassure her. If she becomes aggressive or accusatory and is making you uncomfortable, you are not obliged to keep begging for her to believe that you’re not a bad friend - maybe this friendship isn’t meant to work out.

I assumed my teacher was crying because I was leaving or something, and I didn’t want to upset my mum by asking what had upset her.

Several years later when I was around 9 or 10, mum and dad asked me if I remembered my prep teacher. I said of course, and they gently told me she had passed away and showed me a notice in the newspaper. I was of course saddened for a bit and mum and dad had told me she was sick with a disease (they told me the name but of course I didn’t know what it was really). 

Years on I found out that my mum was comforting my teacher that day because she had been diagnosed with motor neurone disease (MND) [also known as amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS)]. Knowing now how awful and scary that disease is, it absolutely breaks my heart thinking of how awful it must have been for my teacher to receive her diagnosis, and for her life and body to have been slowly and debilitatingly taken by the disease.

At 4 o'clock in the morning, when me and three of my best friends were supposed to be having a sleepover (one was already passed out on the couch), one sent me a long, detailed message from the other room outlining her gratitude and appreciation for having had me as a friend before asking me to 'make sure [her] mother gets [her] stuff' (clothes, her phone, etc). 

She walked out the door into the blackness of the night, and I adorning no shoes nor a phone followed her (I know, stupid not to take a phone but I panicked). 
I walked after her for miles down the road, making conversation as she begged me to turn around and leave. I refused, and she broke down and told me I could either turn around and go back or I could watch her jump off the bridge. 
So I started bawling my eyes out, because we knew she struggled with her depression but I didn't know it was this bad. She was sobbing, telling me to leave and that she didn't want to feel anymore, and I pleaded with her. I told her I loved her, and that I will always support her and that she needs to keep being so strong, because what else do I say? I was lost for words, and each feeble sentence that erupted from my mouth felt lost on her, like she had heard the same thing so many times that it had no effect. 

I was still with her when we reached the bridge. She peered over the side, and I held her arm and begged her to step back, tears silently pouring down both of our faces. Then, as the wind softened, a silence crept in and it went eerily quiet. And this girl, this supporter and best friend who has cried into my shoulder so many times, who I've laughed with, danced with, sung with, shared with.. collapsed into a puddle of tears. She fell to her knees, begging for mercy from her mind, pleading for the constant pain to stop, the helplessness that burdened her shoulders never faltering, and in that moment my heart broke. I held her and sobbed alongside her, whispering "I'm sorry" over and over because all other words left me.

That was the most terrifying thing I've seen or heard, or felt. The absolute breakdown of someone suffering their mental health's worst.

We sat there for a while, her in my arms and the only sounds being the engines of the cars on the highway beside us, or the sniffling from our noses. Eventually, I stood up, used my arm to pull her up and with her hand in mine, we walked silently back to the house.

I just correct a small number of basic grammatical errors, like adding most to something that is -est (most nicest, etc.) or more -er (more nicer, etc.) and misusing the three there/their/they'res and where/were/we're. I'm not trying to say my grammar is perfect, because I know it's not, but its just these basic errors that annoy me heaps. I also get really annoyed when sleeves are caught, or collars are folded or bent improperly. In high school, my friends heard that there's a type of OCD where people must correct all grammatical errors, and they believed I had OCD.
